title: Σφῆκες καὶ πέρδικες καὶ γεωργός
titleEn: The Wasps, the Partridges and the Farmer
part: The Wasps, the Partridges and the Farmer (Chambry 330 · Perry 215)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 330 (= Perry 215). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Σφῆκες καὶ πέρδικες δίψῃ συνεχόμενοι πρὸς γεωργὸν ἦλθον παρ’ αὐτοῦ αἰτοῦντες πιεῖν, ἐπαγγελλόμενοι ἀντὶ τοῦ ὕδατος ταύτην τὴν χάριν ἀποδώσειν· οἱ μὲν πέρδικες σκάπτειν τὰς ἀμπέλους, οἱ δὲ σφῆκες κύκλῳ περιιόντες τοῖς κέντροις ἀποσοβεῖν τοὺς κλέπτας.
sentences.tr: Sphēkes kai perdikes dipsēi synechomenoi pros geōrgon ēlthon par’ autou aitountes piein, epangellomenoi anti tou hydatos tautēn tēn charin apodōsein· hoi men perdikes skaptein tas ampelous, hoi de sphēkes kyklōi periiontes tois kentrois aposobein tous kleptas.
sentences.l: Wasps and partridges, being gripped by thirst, came to a farmer asking of him to drink, promising to repay this favour in return for the water: the partridges to dig about the vines, and the wasps, going round in a circle, to drive off thieves with their stings.
sentences.i: Wasps and partridges, held fast by thirst, came to a farmer and asked him for a drink, promising to repay the favour of the water — the partridges to dig about his vines, the wasps to go the rounds and drive thieves off with their stings.
sentences.n: συνέχομαι is to be held fast, gripped: the regular verb for being in the grip of thirst or of a disease. The two future infinitives after ἐπαγγελλόμενοι carry what each party undertakes, with μέν … δέ dividing the offers. σκάπτω is to dig round the vine-stocks, the vine-dresser's standing labour; ἄμπελος is strictly the vine, but here stands for the whole planting.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ γεωργὸς ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ἔμοιγέ εἰσι δύο βόες, οἳ μηδὲν ἐπαγγελλόμενοι πάντα ποιοῦσιν· ἄμεινον οὖν ἐστιν ἐκείνοις δοῦναι ἤπερ ὑμῖν. »
sentences.tr: Ho de geōrgos ephē· « All’ emoige eisi dyo boes, hoi mēden epangellomenoi panta poiousin· ameinon oun estin ekeinois dounai ēper hymin. »
sentences.l: And the farmer said: « But to me at any rate there are two oxen, who, promising nothing, do everything; it is better, then, to give to them than to you. »
sentences.i: And the farmer said: « But I have two oxen, and they promise nothing and do everything. Better, then, to give the water to them than to you. »
sentences.n: ἔμοιγε … εἰσι is the dative of possession, 'to me there are two oxen' — Greek's usual way of saying 'I have'. ἤπερ is ἤ strengthened by the particle, 'than … at any rate'. The oxen are not thirstier; they simply never made an offer.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος πρὸς ἄνδρας ἐξώλεις ὠφελεῖν μὲν ἐπαγγελλομένους, βλάπτοντας δὲ μεγάλα.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos pros andras exōleis ōphelein men epangellomenous, blaptontas de megala.
sentences.l: The fable is directed at utterly worthless men who promise to help but do great harm.
sentences.n: ἐξώλης is 'ruined, past saving', and as a term of abuse it is about as strong as Greek gets. μεγάλα is a neuter adjective standing as an internal accusative with βλάπτοντας, 'do great harm'; the μέν … δέ sets the promise against the performance.
